questions.text:
Consider the following languages:

I. [latex] \{a^{m}b^{n}c^{p}d^{q}|m+p=n+q, \; where \; m,n,p,q \geq 0 \}[/latex]
II. [latex]\{a^{m}b^{n}c^{p}d^{q}|m=n \; and \; p=q, \; where \; m,n,p,q\geq 0 \} [/latex]
III. [latex] \{a^{m}b^{n}c^{p}d^{q}|m=n=p \; and \; p\neq q, \; where \; m,n,p,q\geq 0 \} [/latex]
IV. [latex]\{a^{m}b^{n}c^{p}d^{q}|mn=p+q, \; where\; m,n,p,q\geq 0\}[/latex]

Which of the languages above are context-free?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- I: m + p = n + q needs only one counter (a's and c's add, b's and d's subtract) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] CFL True
- II: [latex]a^mb^mc^pd^p[/latex]: two independent matches in sequence [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] CFL True
- III: m = n = p needs three equal counts [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not CFL
- IV: mn = p + q needs multiplication [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not CFL

Answer: I and II only

questions.text: The set of all recursively enumerable languages is
questions.solution:
RE languages are closed under intersection (run both TMs; accept when both accept). They are not closed under complement, are a superset (not subset) of recursive languages, and are countable (TMs can be listed).

Answer: closed under intersection

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: a subset of the set of all recursive languages.

questions.text: Let N be an NFA with n states. Let k be the number of states of a minimal DFA which is equivalent to N. Which one of the following is necessarily true?
questions.solution:
The subset construction turns an n-state NFA into a DFA whose states are subsets of the NFA's states, at most [latex]2^n[/latex]. The minimal DFA cannot be bigger, but it can be much smaller (so the other bounds are not guaranteed).

Answer: [latex]k\le2^n[/latex]

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

questions.text: If L and P are two recursively enumerable languages then they are not closed under
questions.solution:
RE languages are closed under union, intersection and Kleene star, but not under complement, so not under set difference ([latex]L-P=L\cap\bar P[/latex]).

Answer: Set difference

questions.text: In some programming language, an identifier is permitted to be a letter followed by any number of letters or digits. If [latex]L[/latex] and [latex]D[/latex] denote the sets of letters and digits respectively, which of the following expressions defines an identifier?
questions.solution:
One letter, followed by any number of letters or digits: [latex]L(L+D)^*[/latex].

Answer: [latex]L(L+D)^*[/latex]
